```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 150, out.width = "100%")
```

Joinpoint regression assumes that the mean changes smoothly, with occasional
changes of slope. Two kinds of events break that assumption: one-off
anomalies, such as a pandemic year, and changes in how the outcome is
recorded, such as a new revision of the International Classification of
Diseases (ICD). Left alone, both distort the trend estimates. This vignette
shows how to handle each.

```{r}
library(joinpoint)
library(ggplot2)
```

## A one-off anomaly: 1918

The 1918 influenza pandemic more than doubled mortality from influenza and
pneumonia for a single year. A least squares fit treats that year as information
about the trend:

```{r, fig.alt = "Influenza and pneumonia death rate by year, 1900 to 1998, on a logarithmic axis with the fitted joinpoint model; the 1918 pandemic stands out as a single spike."}
flu <- subset(us_mortality, cause == "Influenza and Pneumonia")
fit_all <- joinpoint(flu, year, rate, kmax = 3, ci_method = "parametric")
autoplot(fit_all, log_y = TRUE)
```

The joinpoints, in 1936 and 1950, are not driven by 1918, but the single
outlier inflates the residual variance and with it every interval. An
excluded year is left out of the fit but kept in the data and the graph,
drawn as a hollow point:

```{r, fig.alt = "The influenza and pneumonia series fitted without 1918, on a logarithmic axis; the excluded 1918 value is drawn as a hollow point."}
fit_ex <- joinpoint(flu, year, rate, kmax = 3, exclude = 1918,
                    ci_method = "parametric")
autoplot(fit_ex, log_y = TRUE)
merge(apc(fit_all)[, c("segment", "lower", "upper")],
      apc(fit_ex)[, c("segment", "lower", "upper")],
      by = "segment", suffixes = c("_all", "_without_1918"))
```

Without 1918 the intervals are about a fifth narrower. Exclusion is a
statement that the year does not belong to the trend. It should be
justified by external knowledge, as here, not by the size of the residual.
The same tool handles the drop of cancer diagnoses in 2020, when screening
was interrupted.

## A coding change: the jump model

When the ICD changes, deaths move between categories overnight. The trend
continues, but its level shifts. The jump model (Chen et al. 2020) adds a
discontinuity halfway between the last year of the old coding and the first
year of the new one and estimates its size along with the joinpoints. The
ratio of rates after and before the change is the comparability ratio.

ICD-9 replaced ICD-8 in the United States in 1979. The jump model estimates
the effect of this change on heart disease mortality:

```{r, fig.alt = "Heart disease death rate by year from 1950 with a joinpoint model that allows a jump at the 1978 coding change, marked by a dotted vertical line labeled with the comparability ratio; the fitted line steps up at 1978."}
heart <- subset(us_mortality, cause == "Heart Disease" & year >= 1950)
fit_jump <- joinpoint(heart, year, rate, kmax = 3, jump = 1978,
                      ci_method = "parametric")
jump_estimates(fit_jump)[, c("statistic", "estimate", "lower", "upper",
                             "p_value")]
autoplot(fit_jump)
```

The estimated comparability ratio of about 1.03 says that heart disease
death rates were about 3% higher under ICD-9 than they would have been
under ICD-8, and its confidence interval excludes 1. Ignoring the change
would have blurred the trend around 1979.

A jump estimated close to a joinpoint is confounded with the change of
slope. For tuberculosis the model places a joinpoint at 1978, the last
year of the old coding, right next to the jump at 1978.5:

```{r}
tbc <- subset(us_mortality, cause == "Tuberculosis" & year >= 1950)
fit_tb <- joinpoint(tbc, year, rate, kmax = 3, jump = 1978,
                    ci_method = "parametric")
joinpoints(fit_tb)$estimate
jump_estimates(fit_tb)[, c("statistic", "estimate", "se")]
```

In the separate segment regressions used for standard errors, the jump then
coincides with the start of a segment and cannot be separated from its
intercept, so no standard error is available. Such a jump estimate should
not be reported.

## A known comparability ratio

When a bridge coding study has estimated the comparability ratio, it can be
supplied instead of estimated. The rates before the change are multiplied
by the ratio (with their standard errors updated by the delta method when
standard errors are used), the model is fitted to the converted series, and
fitted values before the change are divided back for display. The ratio
below is illustrative, chosen to match the jump model estimate, not a
published value.

```{r}
fit_cr <- joinpoint(heart, year, rate, kmax = 3, jump = 1978,
                    comparability_ratio = 1.03, ci_method = "parametric")
apc(fit_cr)[, c("start", "end", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
```

A ratio from a double coding study of a similar population is the safer
choice. When no such study exists, the jump model estimates the ratio from
the series itself, at the price of confounding with any change of slope
near the coding change.

## Reference

Chen HS, Zeichner S, Anderson RN, Espey DK, Kim HJ, Feuer EJ (2020). The
joinpoint-jump and joinpoint-comparability ratio model for trend analysis
with applications to coding changes in health statistics. *Journal of
Official Statistics* 36:49-62.
